name: Battir
tagline: A stone village above a valley of ancient irrigated terraces, still farmed and still watered by a spring-fed system shared out among the village's families for centuries.
highlight: The valley floor walk along the ancient irrigation channels, with olive, fig and vegetable terraces on one side and the old railway on the other.
shortDescription: A UNESCO-listed farming village near Bethlehem, known for its terraced valley, its shared irrigation and its small green aubergines, and a gentle place to walk.
metaDescription: A Battir travel guide: the UNESCO terraced landscape, the spring and irrigation system, the walk through the valley, the Ottoman railway, village food and a half-day plan from Bethlehem.
nearestAirport: Tel Aviv Ben Gurion (TLV), about 1 hour 15 minutes; Bethlehem is 10 km away
knownFor: Terraced farming landscape, ancient irrigation, hiking, local food
goodFor: Walking, landscape, agriculture, a quiet half-day from Bethlehem

image.alt: The stone houses of Battir above their terraced valley

intro: Battir is a small village of about 4,000 people, seven kilometres west of Bethlehem, on the edge of a steep valley called Wadi al-Makhrour. The valley is terraced with dry-stone walls that hold small plots of olives, vines, figs, almonds and vegetables. It is watered by springs, and by an irrigation system that has been in use since Roman times, and that is shared among the village's families in a rotating schedule that has hardly changed in centuries.

In 2014, UNESCO inscribed the landscape as 'Palestine: Land of Olives and Vines, Cultural Landscape of Southern Jerusalem, Battir', and put it on the List in Danger because of the threat from planned development and the separation barrier. The Palestinian community and Israeli conservation groups jointly challenged the route of the barrier through the valley in the courts, and the case became a symbol of community-led heritage protection.

At the bottom of the valley runs the old Jaffa–Jerusalem railway, built by the Ottomans in 1892, where trains still pass. The village is a quiet, green place to walk, and the trails through the terraces are an easy half-day. It is small, quiet and a welcome contrast to the noise of the cities.

whyVisit.intro: Battir is a place to walk, look and slow down, and it shows a side of Palestine that is rarely on the news.

points.title: An ancient landscape still in use
points.text: The terraces and irrigation system are not a reconstruction or a museum piece. Families still farm them and share the water.

points.title: An easy and beautiful walk
points.text: The trails through the valley are a couple of hours, mostly flat, and pass springs, pools and old farm buildings.

points.title: A village cooperative
points.text: Local guides, cafés and a small eco-museum offer visitors a warm welcome, and income goes to the community.

points.title: Battiri aubergines
points.text: The village is famous for its small, sweet aubergines, grown in the terraces and served in local dishes.

points.title: Close to Bethlehem
points.text: Only 10–15 minutes by car, so it fits into a day with the Church of the Nativity.

attractionsIntro: Battir is small, and a visit takes two to four hours. A local guide adds a lot.

attractions.name: The terraced valley

image.alt: The terraced fields and olive trees in the Battir valley

attractions.text: Wadi al-Makhrour, the valley of Battir, is a stepped hillside of stone terraces, planted with olives, fruit trees and vegetables. The paths that run along it are easy to follow.
attractions.tip: Go in spring or autumn, when the terraces are green and the light is soft.

attractions.name: The Roman-era irrigation system
attractions.text: A network of channels and pools, fed by a spring called Ain al-Balad, that delivers water to each family's plot in turn. The system dates from Roman times and is still managed by the families.
attractions.tip: Ask a guide to explain how the turns work.

attractions.name: The Ottoman railway
attractions.text: The Jaffa–Jerusalem line, opened in 1892, runs along the bottom of the valley through a small station. Trains still use it, and a walking path follows the tracks.
attractions.tip: Trains run at times, so stay off the tracks and listen.

attractions.name: The village and its old houses
attractions.text: Stone houses with arched doors and flat roofs, old olive presses and a small mosque line the village lanes. The centre is quiet and friendly.

attractions.name: The Battir Eco-Museum and visitor centre
attractions.text: A small centre run by the local community, with displays on the landscape, the irrigation system and village life, and a base for guided walks.

attractions.name: Walking trails to Bethlehem and Wadi Fukin
attractions.text: Longer routes follow the terraces to nearby villages and hills, including sections of the Masar Ibrahim al-Khalil walking trail.
attractions.tip: Check the route and conditions with a local guide.

thingsToDoIntro: Battir is small, and a slow visit works best.

thingsToDo.title: Walk the valley
thingsToDo.text: A two-hour circuit along the terraces, springs and railway is the highlight of a visit.
thingsToDo.tip: Wear sturdy shoes and bring water.

thingsToDo.title: Hire a local guide
thingsToDo.text: Guides from the village explain the irrigation system, the history and the politics of the area.
thingsToDo.tip: Book through the eco-museum or your accommodation.

thingsToDo.title: Have lunch in the village
thingsToDo.text: Village restaurants and homes serve local dishes, including the famous Battir aubergine, with olive oil, herbs and bread.
thingsToDo.tip: Ask in advance for a home-cooked meal.

thingsToDo.title: Pick fruit or help with the harvest
thingsToDo.text: In season, visitors can join families in the olive harvest or fruit picking.

thingsToDo.title: Visit in spring
thingsToDo.text: The terraces are green, the flowers are out, and the light is soft.
thingsToDo.tip: March and April are the best months.

thingsToDo.title: Combine with Bethlehem
thingsToDo.text: A morning at the Church of the Nativity and an afternoon in Battir make a satisfying day.
thingsToDo.tip: Hire a driver for the day.

foodIntro: Food in Battir is simple and rural, based on the produce of the terraces.

foods.name: Battiri aubergine
foods.text: A small, sweet, thin-skinned aubergine, grown for centuries in the valley, and served stuffed, grilled or in stews.

foods.name: Village mezze
foods.text: Salads, dips, olives and cheeses made from local produce, with freshly baked bread.
foods.whereToTry: Restaurants and homes in the village.

foods.name: Musakhan
foods.text: Roast chicken on taboon bread with sumac and onions, especially in the olive-harvest season.

foods.name: Olive oil
foods.text: The village's olive trees produce a fragrant, peppery oil, sold in bottles and used in everything.

foods.name: Fresh fruit and figs
foods.text: Figs, grapes and almonds are picked in season.

accommodation.intro: Most visitors come for a half-day from Bethlehem, but a few guesthouses in Battir and the nearby villages welcome overnight guests.

areas.name: Battir village
areas.text: Simple guesthouses and a homestay run by local families.

areas.name: Bethlehem
areas.text: A wider choice of hotels and restaurants, 15 minutes away.

gettingThere.intro: Battir is about 7 km west of Bethlehem, and a taxi is the easiest way there.

options.text: A short drive of 15 minutes. Taxis can wait or come back for you.
options.detail: Agree the fare and the return time.

options.text: Many tours combine Battir with Bethlehem and other sites.
A walking trail links the two, mostly through hills and villages, and takes about four hours.

gettingAround.intro: Everything is on foot in the valley and the village.

options.text: The valley paths are well defined and mostly flat, with a few steps.
A guide from the village leads groups along the terraces and irrigation channels.
Useful for the journey to the village and to nearby sites.

bestTime.headline: March–May and September–November
bestTime.summary: Battir is in the hills at about 700 m. Spring and autumn are the best seasons for walking, and winter can be cold and wet.

seasons.text: Green terraces and wildflowers. The best time.
Warm and dry. Walk early or late.
Warm and clear, with the olive harvest in October and November.
Cool and wet. Paths can be muddy.

bestTime.avoid: Rainy days, when paths are slippery, and days of unrest.

itinerary.title: Half a day in Battir
itinerary.intro: A guided walk in the morning and a village lunch. Assumes a driver from Bethlehem.

days.title: Terraces and lunch
days.morning: A guided walk through the terraces and along the railway.
days.afternoon: A home-cooked lunch in the village, then a visit to the eco-museum.
days.evening: Back in Bethlehem for the evening.

tipsIntro: Battir is quiet and small, and a few tips help.
tips: Go with a local guide. It adds a lot, and it supports the village.
Wear sturdy shoes, and take water and a hat.
Respect the terraces. Stay on the paths, and do not climb on the walls or pick fruit without permission.
Stay off the railway tracks. Trains still pass.
Buy olive oil and local products from the village cooperatives.
Check conditions before you go. Battir is close to the barrier and checkpoints, and access can change.
Combine it with Bethlehem for a full day.

faq.q: Why is Battir a UNESCO site?
faq.a: For its ancient terraced landscape and irrigation system, which have been used and managed by local families for centuries. It was inscribed in 2014 and placed on the List in Danger.

faq.q: How long do you need in Battir?
faq.a: Half a day is enough for a guided walk and lunch. A night in the village is a quiet and relaxing addition.
It is not required, but a local guide adds a great deal and supports the community. Book in advance.

faq.q: Is Battir easy to reach from Bethlehem?
faq.a: Yes. It is about 15 minutes by taxi, and is often combined with the Church of the Nativity. You can also walk between them with a guide.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit?
faq.a: March to May and September to November. Spring is greenest, and autumn brings the olive harvest.
Its terraces, its irrigation system and its small green aubergines, known as Battiri aubergines.
